extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, and IP practitioners interested in Korean patent administrative procedures (KIPO/IPTAB)
extracted.subtask_description: Description of the structure, types, procedures, timelines, and legal effects of administrative patent trials and appeals handled by the Korean Intellectual Property Trial and Appeal Board (IPTAB) and their relationship with judicial revocation suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of IPTAB proceedings (ex parte and inter partes)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two types of IPTAB proceedings: ex parte and inter partes. An ex parte case is an appeal against an examiner’s decision to reject an application and involves only the petitioner. In inter partes cases, a petitioner and a defendant dispute over a granted right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification to determine procedure and parties' rights; note that from March 2017 the IPTAB also started hearing 'patent opposition' challenges ex parte.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte case categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex parte proceedings include: appeal against a decision to reject an application; trial for correction; patent opposition (since March 2017).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies which remedial routes are handled without an opposing party present; practitioners should choose ex parte route where appropriate and be aware of the inclusion of patent opposition as ex parte since 2017.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter partes case categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter partes proceedings include: trial for invalidation; trial to confirm the scope of rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These proceedings require opposing parties (petitioner and defendant) and are used when disputed rights are already granted or when scope/validity is contested between parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal period for a decision to reject an application
rubrics_metrics.description: When an applicant receives a decision of rejection from an examiner, they may pursue an appeal within 30 days of the date of receipt of the certified copy of the decision (Article 132-17 of the Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict 30-day deadline from receipt of certified copy; timely filing is jurisdictional. Reference the cited article when preparing procedural calendars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted grounds for a trial for correction
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent holder may pursue a petition for the correction of a granted patent or utility model for the reasons of narrowing a claim, correcting a clerical error, or clarifying an ambiguous description (Article 136 of the Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correction petitions are limited to specified grounds—requests outside narrowing/clerical/clarifying grounds likely to be dismissed. Draft correction requests narrowly to fit statutory reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial for invalidation (standing and basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: An interested party may seek a trial to retroactively invalidate the granted patent right based on statutory invalidation grounds (Article 133 of the Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires an 'interested party' and reliance on statutory invalidation grounds; use this route to attack validity of a granted patent with retroactive effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial to confirm the scope of rights (standing)
rubrics_metrics.description: An interested party may seek a trial to confirm whether a technology that is being practiced or will be practiced by a third party falls within the scope of a granted patent (Article 135 of the Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used proactively or defensively to determine infringement scope; standing requires interest in the question of whether particular technology is covered by the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent opposition timing and basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person may request a patent opposition, within six months of the publication of the grant of the patent, to revoke the patent based on prior art (Article 132-2 of the Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Six-month deadline from grant publication is strict; opposition is available to 'any person' and is specifically targeted at prior-art-based revocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing format and oral hearing conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearings may be held orally or in writing. Unless requested otherwise, hearings are conducted generally in writing. An oral hearing is held upon request from the parties or if the presiding administrative judge finds it necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default is written proceedings—request oral hearing if factual/legal presentation would benefit; judges may independently order oral hearings where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition and decision rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A panel of three or five administrative judges hears a case and participates in deliberations to reach a conclusion by a majority vote before rendering the final decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect multi-judge panels and majority-rule outcomes; prepare arguments and evidence knowing multiple judges will deliberate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal route from IPTAB decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant who is dissatisfied with the final decision of the IPTAB may appeal to the Patent Court. A Patent Court decision is appealed to the Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative IPTAB route is not the end point—judicial review is available in the Patent Court and then Supreme Court; plan for potential multi-stage litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non bis in idem effect of final IPTAB decisions and exception for rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If an IPTAB decision on a case becomes final and conclusive, no person may demand a retrial based on the same facts or evidence. However, this requirement does not apply where the final and conclusive ruling is a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final IPTAB rulings generally bar relitigation on the same facts/evidence; be aware that a final rejection does not trigger the bar—other procedural consequences differ between outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and scope of 'same facts' and 'same evidence' under non bis in idem
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'same facts' means certain facts that stem from the same cause with respect to the same right; different causes (e.g., lack of novelty, inventive step, industrial usability) that all result in invalidity are treated as separate facts. 'Same evidence' includes evidence submitted before a previously confirmed IPTAB decision and any supplementary evidence that is not compelling enough to overturn the confirmed decision; new evidence that is compelling enough to overturn is not in breach of the non bis in idem principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing preclusion, analyze whether the new proceeding relies on materially different facts or genuinely new and compelling evidence; novelty vs inventive_step vs utility are separate factual bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship and procedural distinction between revocation suits and administrative patent trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Litigation for the revocation of an IPTAB decision is a judicial process carried out by the Patent Court under the adversarial system and the principle of pleadings. Administrative patent trials are administrative appeal procedures handled by the IPTAB under the inquisitorial system. IPTAB trials are fundamentally different from judicial appellate proceedings and are not linked in terms of instance; arguments or materials presented in an IPTAB trial cannot be automatically treated as presented in a revocation suit in court because the latter requires arguments and materials to be newly presented or submitted for the court to consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that materials filed before the IPTAB will be treated as already submitted in a subsequent revocation suit—prepare to replead and resubmit materials for the court; tailor strategy to adversarial vs inquisitorial processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPTAB institutional structure and division roles
rubrics_metrics.description: The IPTAB has three divisions: Appeals boards (handle trials and appeals related to rejection of applications, invalidation and cancellation of registrations, corrections, and confirmation of scope), a Litigation division (represents the Commissioner of the KIPO in revocation suits in the Patent Court), and a Trial Policy division (oversees general affairs relating to the operation of the IPTAB). Appeals boards consist of a panel of three administrative judges, each in charge of a specific area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding internal IPTAB structure helps identify which division/board will handle a matter and who represents the KIPO in subsequent judicial proceedings; anticipate specialized panels for specific subject areas.
